This is the working order I want to follow on a new dataset. It is assembled from
the weekly coding homework in CMU **24-887 — Machine Learning & AI for
Engineers**: each week taught one piece (a scaler, a model family, k-fold, PCA,
an ensemble), and this page puts those pieces into one loop.

A reminder of which lecture introduced each idea is on the
[lecture concepts](../lecture-concepts/index.qmd) page. The derivations live
elsewhere: [logistic regression](../logistic-regression/index.qmd),

## The loop

Hold out a test set first. Every choice after that — which columns, which scaler,
which model, which hyperparameters — is made on the training rows and checked
with k-fold. The test set is scored once, after the choice is fixed.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A["Frame the job<br/>regression, classification, or no labels"] --> B["Look at the columns<br/>histograms, correlation, a few raw plots"]
  B --> C["Hold out a test set<br/>and do not tune on it"]
  C --> D["Build pipelines<br/>scale, expand, select, then the model"]
  D --> E["Compare models and hyperparameters<br/>with k-fold on the training set"]
  E --> F{"Validation score<br/>still moving?"}
  F -->|yes| D
  F -->|no| G["Optional ensemble<br/>bagging, boosting, stacking"]
  G --> H["Refit the winner on all training rows"]
  H --> I["Score the test set once<br/>and plot the errors"]
```

Three habits make the score mean something.

1. **Fit every transform on the training side of the current split.** A
   `Pipeline` does this on each fold. In the week 6 scaling exercise the test
   rows were scaled with the min and max of the *training* matrix, so a test
   value landed above 1. That is the correct behavior. Computing min, max,
   mean, variance, quantiles, PCA axes, or a correlation filter on the full
   table leaks the test rows into the transform.
2. **Read the training score and the validation score together.** On the
   cylinder-bands data, one decision tree (`max_depth=10`) reached 93% training
   accuracy and 66% test accuracy. A random forest of 100 such trees reached
   100% and 82%. On the nodal-stress XGBoost sweep, `eta=0.7` and `max_depth=20`
   drove training MSE to $7.4 \times 10^{-6}$ while test MSE was
   $6.0 \times 10^{-3}$. The best test MSE in that grid was
   $4.6 \times 10^{-3}$, at `eta=0.3` and `max_depth=15`. The lowest training
   error was a worse model.
3. **Average more than one split.** In the week 10 neural-net study, 100 epochs
   underfit, 2000 epochs overfit, and 500 was the best of the three by average
   test MSE. Inside that best setting the five folds still ranged from about
   0.16 to 0.21. A single 80/20 cut would have picked a winner that another cut
   disagreed with.

The XGBoost grid above was scored on the test set, because that is what the
exercise asked. The same grid at work goes through `GridSearchCV` on the
training split. The test set stays out of the search.

## 1. Frame the job

| I have | I fit | I report |
|---|---|---|
| A number to predict | A regressor | MSE, and $R^2$ when I want a unitless comparison |
| A class label | A classifier | Accuracy, plus a confusion matrix once the model is chosen |
| No label, and I need groups or a view of the points | DBSCAN, or PCA / t-SNE | The picture, and a downstream supervised score only if labels show up later |

MSE and accuracy both get printed on the training rows and on the held-out
rows. The confusion matrix is a one-time picture of *which* classes trade off,
after the model is chosen. Week 9 used it on MNIST; week 11 used it on a
classifier checked after clustering-style image work.

## 2. Look at the columns before fitting

Plot a histogram of each column on the training rows, and a scatter of the
target against any column that might dominate. On the week 6 concrete-strength
sheet, those histograms were what made the later scaling change intelligible:
quantile scaling cut the degree-3 linear model's test MSE from 59.4 to 32.7.

Then drop a column that repeats another one. Pearson filtering, as coded in
week 6: take the absolute correlation of the training columns, and when two
features correlate above a threshold, drop the one with the weaker correlation
to the target.

```python
import numpy as np

def redundant_feature_indices(X, y, threshold=0.9):
    """Indices of columns to drop. X and y are training rows only."""
    data = np.column_stack([y, X])
    corr = np.abs(np.corrcoef(data.T))
    remove = []
    for i, j in zip(*np.triu_indices(corr.shape[0], k=1)):
        if i == 0 or corr[i, j] <= threshold:
            continue
        # columns i and j of `data`; feature index in X is that minus 1
        drop = j if corr[i, 0] >= corr[j, 0] else i
        if drop != 0:
            remove.append(drop - 1)
    return sorted(set(remove))
```

A wrapper does the same job with a model in the loop. Recursive feature
elimination (`RFE`) fits an estimator, throws away the weakest column, and
repeats until `n_features_to_select` remain. On the nodal-stress features the
homework kept 30. That count is specific to that table. In the workflow, `RFE`
sits *inside* the pipeline so each fold picks its own columns:

```python
from sklearn.feature_selection import RFE
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

RFE(DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0), n_features_to_select=30)
```

After a fit, read `feature_importances_` on a tree and `coef_` on a linear
model, and plot them. Those plots are how I check that the selector kept the
columns the model actually uses.

## 3. Feature engineering

Each of these is a step in a pipeline, fitted on training rows.

### Scaling

Per column, from the training rows:

| Transform | Formula | What it did in the homework |
|---|---|---|
| Min–max | $(x - x_{\min}) / (x_{\max} - x_{\min})$ | Puts each training column on $[0, 1]$. A test value can fall outside that interval. |
| Standard | $(x - \mu) / \sigma$ | Mean 0, variance 1. The week 8 network's loss did not converge until the inputs were standardized. |
| Quantile | Map the column onto a target distribution (uniform by default) | `QuantileTransformer(n_quantiles=800)` on a 2-D regression. |

Same four models, test MSE, before and after that quantile transform:

| Model | Raw inputs | After quantile scaling |
|---|---:|---:|
| Degree-8 linear regression | 82.8 | 237.3 |
| RBF SVR, $C = 1000$ | 98.6 | 43.0 |
| k-NN, $k = 4$ | 47.6 | 36.4 |
| Random forest, 100 trees, depth 10 | 24.5 | 24.8 |

Distance models (k-NN, RBF SVM) and gradient models (logistic regression, a
neural net) get the scaler. A forest splits on thresholds, so a monotone
rescaling of a column barely moves it. A high-degree linear model can get
*worse* if the scaler is applied to the expanded columns and flattens the
polynomial structure. I try the scaler, I record both scores, and I keep it
only when validation improves.

`StandardScaler` is the default I reach for. `MinMaxScaler` when I want a
bounded range. `QuantileTransformer` when a histogram is badly skewed.

### Expansion

`PolynomialFeatures` builds the products that let a linear model bend.
Week 3 mapped the projectile features before logistic regression. Week 4 put
degree 2 and a `StandardScaler` in front of an SVR. Week 6 used degree 8 in
front of linear regression, and degree 3 on the concrete data.

The step order that matched the homework pipelines:

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

Pipeline([
    ("expand", PolynomialFeatures(degree=3, include_bias=False)),
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("model", Ridge(alpha=1.0)),
])
```

`Ridge` is scikit-learn's form of the week 2 regularized least squares,
$w = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y$, with `alpha` as $\lambda$. A high
degree with $\lambda = 0$ oscillated on the week 2 data; the $L_2$ term pulled
the weights down and smoothed the fit. For logistic regression and `SVC`, the
homework's knob is $C$, and the course relation is $\lambda = 1/C$.

### Dimensionality reduction

PCA builds an orthogonal map. Fit it on the training rows (after scaling, when
the columns have different units), choose the dimension from the cumulative
explained variance, and check the result by reconstructing.

On the 64×64 signed-distance fields (4096 columns, 8 classes):

- 9 components explained more than 90% of the *training* variance.
- Reconstructing with all components is exact for a training row. A test row
  can still miss detail, because its variance was not in the fit.
- k-NN accuracy on the test set was 0.71 in 3-D, 0.90 in 10-D, and 0.93 in
  50-D. The variance curve and the accuracy curve are both worth plotting;
  90% variance was not the same operating point as the best classifier.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

pca = PCA().fit(X_train_scaled)
cumulative = np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
n_for_90 = int(np.searchsorted(cumulative, 0.9) + 1)
```

In the pipeline, `PCA(n_components=n_for_90)` is just another step. A later
sample is mapped with `transform`.

t-SNE is the picture of points I already have (`TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30)`
in the homework, after a 50-D PCA). It has no `transform` for a row that was
absent from the fit. The homework embedded the full SDF table and then split,
so the k-NN accuracy on that embedding describes the picture, and it is the
wrong number to quote for a part that arrives next month. I use t-SNE to see
whether the classes separate. I use PCA when the reduced coordinates have to
be computed for a new row.

### Different transforms on different columns

`ColumnTransformer` is the week 6 pattern for a table whose columns want
different treatment. Columns left out of the list pass through.

```python
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import QuantileTransformer

preprocess = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        ("standard", StandardScaler(), [0, 3, 6, 7, 8]),
        ("quantile", QuantileTransformer(n_quantiles=10), [1, 2, 5, 9]),
    ],
    remainder="passthrough",
)
```

A transform I write myself goes in as a `FunctionTransformer`, which is how
week 6 chained a hand-written step with an SVR. It has to be a pure function
of the rows it is given, because the pipeline will call it on each fold.

## 4. Models I actually compare

I put several of these in one search and let the validation score choose. The
defaults below are the settings the homework started from, and they are
starting points for the grid in the next section.

| Family | Estimator | When it earned a place | Knobs the homework turned |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linear | `LinearRegression`, `Ridge`, `LogisticRegression` | First baseline, and the model behind polynomial expansion | Polynomial degree, `alpha` or `C` |
| Support vector | `SVR`, `SVC` | Distance geometry matters and the table is not huge | `kernel` (`linear`, `rbf`), `C` |
| Neighbors | `KNeighborsRegressor`, `KNeighborsClassifier` | A local baseline, including after PCA | `n_neighbors` |
| Tree | `DecisionTreeRegressor`, `DecisionTreeClassifier` | A single tree, mostly as the unit inside a forest | `max_depth` |
| Forest | `RandomForestRegressor`, `RandomForestClassifier` | The tabular default in this course | `n_estimators`, `max_depth` |
| Boosting | `XGBRegressor` | The stress field, after forests and stacking | `eta` (learning rate), `max_depth`, `n_estimators` |
| Neural net | `MLPRegressor` for a quick try; PyTorch when I need the training curve | The target is a smooth function of a few inputs, or an image | Depth, width, epochs, learning rate. Standardize first. |

For a PyTorch net, the week 10 shape is a useful small-regression starting
point: fully connected, widths `[64, 128, 128, 64]`, `tanh` on the hidden
layers, no activation on a regression output, `Adam` at learning rate `0.01`,
`MSELoss`. Classification uses a loss such as cross-entropy and reads accuracy
off the predicted class. The architecture notes are in
[neural networks](../neural-networks/index.qmd).

## 5. One search over models and hyperparameters

This is the week 10 pattern: one pipeline, a list of parameter grids, and
`GridSearchCV` with shuffled 5-fold. Each dict in the list replaces the model
step, so k-NN, SVR, and a forest are compared under the same splits. The
search refits the winning pipeline on all of `X_train`.

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, KFold, train_test_split
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.svm import SVR
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0
)

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("model", KNeighborsRegressor()),
])

param_grid = [
    {
        "model": [KNeighborsRegressor()],
        "model__n_neighbors": [3, 5, 7],
    },
    {
        "model": [SVR()],
        "model__kernel": ["linear", "rbf"],
        "model__C": [0.1, 1, 10],
    },
    {
        "model": [RandomForestRegressor(random_state=0)],
        "model__n_estimators": [100, 200],
        "model__max_depth": [5, 10],
        "scale": ["passthrough"],  # a forest does not need the scaler
    },
]

search = GridSearchCV(
    pipe,
    param_grid,
    cv=KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0),
    scoring="r2",
)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(search.best_params_)
pred = search.best_estimator_.predict(X_test)
print(mean_squared_error(y_test, pred))
```

`"scale": ["passthrough"]` turns that step into the identity for the forest
only. For a classifier I switch the estimators to their `Classifier`
counterparts and set `scoring="accuracy"`.

`cv_results_` has the mean and standard deviation of the score on every
setting. I look at both before I accept the winner. A setting that wins by a
hair, with a large spread across folds, is a weak winner.

Adding expansion or PCA is another step in `pipe`, with its own grid entries
(`expand__degree`, `pca__n_components`). Anything I would otherwise fit on the
whole training matrix before calling `fit` belongs in that list, or the folds
share information.

## 6. K-fold when the model is a training loop

`GridSearchCV` fits anything with `fit` and `predict`. A PyTorch loop needs
the fold indices explicitly. Week 10 used two nested splits:

- The outer `KFold` holds out 20% as the fold's test set.
- Inside the other 80%, `train_test_split(..., test_size=0.25)` holds out a
  quarter of *that* block for the validation curve. A quarter of 80% is 20%
  of the original table, so each fit sees about 60% train, 20% validation,
  20% test.

A new network is constructed inside the training function. Reusing one module
object across folds keeps the previous fold's weights.

```python
import numpy as np
import torch
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

folds = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
epoch_grid = [100, 500, 2000]
mse = {n: [] for n in epoch_grid}

for train_idx, test_idx in folds.split(X):
    for n_epoch in epoch_grid:
        model, train_curve, val_curve = train_model(
            X[train_idx], y[train_idx], n_epoch
        )
        pred = model(torch.as_tensor(X[test_idx], dtype=torch.float32))
        mse[n_epoch].append(
            mean_squared_error(y[test_idx], pred.detach().numpy())
        )

for n_epoch, scores in mse.items():
    print(n_epoch, float(np.mean(scores)), float(np.std(scores)))
```

I plot `train_curve` and `val_curve` on the same axes for every fold. The fold
whose validation loss turns up while training loss keeps falling is the one
that memorized. The number I compare across epoch counts is the mean of the
fold test MSEs, not the best single fold.

## 7. Ensembles, after a single model has a score

An ensemble is another row in the comparison, judged by the same validation
metric. I add one when a tuned single model has stopped moving.

**Bagging.** Several copies of one estimator, each fit on a bootstrap sample,
then averaged (regression) or voted (classification). Week 13 on
`make_moons`: one decision tree averaged 0.930 across 5 folds. Bagging that
tree scored 0.927, 0.943, 0.930, 0.953, 0.950, 0.943 at 1, 10, 20, 50, 100,
and 200 estimators. Fifty trees won, and adding more did not keep helping.
`RandomForestClassifier` is this idea with extra randomness in the splits,
which is why it beat the single tree by so much on cylinder bands.

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

BaggingClassifier(
    estimator=DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0),
    n_estimators=50,
    random_state=0,
)
```

**Boosting.** Week 13 fit `XGBRegressor(objective="reg:squarederror", n_estimators=10)`
on the same nodal-stress features and swept `eta` and `max_depth`. Shallow
trees underfit (test MSE $1.3 \times 10^{-2}$ at `eta=0.1`, depth 5). The
deep, aggressive end memorized (training MSE $7.4 \times 10^{-6}$ at
`eta=0.7`, depth 20) and gave a worse test score than the middle of the grid.
I treat `eta`, `max_depth`, and `n_estimators` as grid parameters and pick
them by validation MSE.

**Stacking.** Several different fitted models, then a second model that takes
their predictions as input. Week 13 stacked a linear regression with trees of
depth 12, 16, and 20, and used another linear regression as the final
estimator. Test MSE was $9.8 \times 10^{-3}$ (linear), $8.3 \times 10^{-3}$,
$8.1 \times 10^{-3}$, $8.5 \times 10^{-3}$ (the three trees), and
$6.0 \times 10^{-3}$ for the stack. The stack's training MSE
($2.4 \times 10^{-3}$) was *higher* than the deepest trees. Its test MSE was
the lowest of the group. That is the outcome I want from stacking: a better
held-out score, from a model that is less glued to the training rows.

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import StackingRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

StackingRegressor(
    estimators=[
        ("linear", LinearRegression()),
        ("tree_12", DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=12, random_state=0)),
        ("tree_16", DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=16, random_state=0)),
        ("tree_20", DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=20, random_state=0)),
    ],
    final_estimator=LinearRegression(),
)
```

`StackingRegressor` cross-validates the base models internally when it builds
the final estimator's inputs. I still wrap the whole object in the outer
k-fold of section 5 if I am comparing it with a forest or an XGBoost model.
Otherwise the stack's score and the forest's score come from different splits.

## 8. Pictures, before I trust the number

The score says how far off I am. The picture says whether the errors are in a
place I care about.

| Picture | What I look for |
|---|---|
| Histogram per training column | Skew, a column that is almost constant, units that differ by powers of ten |
| Prediction and ground truth on the same color scale | A stress field, a scatter of predicted vs. true, a 1-D fit drawn through the points |
| `DecisionBoundaryDisplay` | Where a classifier cuts, next to the training points |
| Training and validation loss vs. epoch | Validation rising while training falls |
| Fold scores side by side | One fold carrying the average |
| Confusion matrix | Which classes are exchanged |
| PCA variance bars, and a reconstruction | How many components the signal actually needs |
| t-SNE colored by class | Whether the classes form groups I can see |

For a field on a mesh, week 6 and week 13 plotted ground truth and prediction
as two panels with the color limits taken from the ground truth. Sharing the
limits is what makes a small error look small.

## 9. When there is no label

DBSCAN groups points by density. The homework clustered melt-pool image
coordinates with `DBSCAN(eps=..., min_samples=...)` and judged the result by
the picture: one image wanted `eps=7`, `min_samples=4`; the other wanted
`eps=2`, `min_samples=2`. Those two numbers are the whole model. I sweep them
and keep the clustering whose groups match the structure I can see, and I
expect to retune them when the spacing of a new image changes.

## A short checklist

I copy this to the top of a new notebook and fill it in.

1. Write down the target, the metric, and what a bad error costs.
2. `train_test_split(..., test_size=0.2, random_state=0)`. Plot the training columns.
3. Drop redundant training columns. Note the indices; apply the same drop to the test columns.
4. Build a pipeline: scale (and expand or PCA, if I have a reason), then the model.
5. `GridSearchCV` on the training set, 5 shuffled folds, several families in one `param_grid`.
6. Read mean and spread of the fold scores. Plot errors, not just the scalar.
7. If a single model has stalled, add a forest, a boosted model, or a stack, and compare it in the same search.
8. Refit on all training rows (the search does this for the winner). Score the test set once. Save the fitted pipeline so a new row goes through the same steps.
